utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Ms. Deirdre Montgomery appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Miroslav Cuskic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And -- Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning, General. Before Ms. Korner continues, I remind you of your solemn declaration. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I -- sorry. I assume that you're -- there are no continuing problems, but I would remind you what we said yesterday, that any time it is necessary to take a break, we would accommodate you. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: General, yesterday, towards the end of the session, I was asking how you arrived at your figure of only 3 per cent of the VRS being professionals, which was in the introduction to your report. And you told us that you thought that you got it from the analysis of combat readiness, and you took a copy of that home. So, having read that, can you tell us where you got the figure of 3 per cent?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would kindly ask the Prosecutor to quote the introduction verbatim, rather than paraphrase the sentence in question and turn it about. Because the introductory part of the report says "up to 3 per cent." And it hasn't been put like that to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Um, well, not in my translation it doesn't. Can we have page 3 of the report, the introduction. Oh, sorry, yes. No, no, sorry, the General's own report. 31D2, please. Can we go to page 3 in English, please, and I think it's probably the same page in B/C/S. And could we highlight, please, the bottom half of the second paragraph, paragraph 2. And according to my translation, Mr. Krgovic, it says: "In conditions of war and armed combat, these documents were applied to military and police forces which consisted of mobilised people (only 3 per cent were professionals) ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, General, could you read out, please, so that we can get a translation of the words in your report on that.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, this is what my report says: These documents were applied in conditions of war and armed combat to military and police forces which consisted of mobilised people (only up to 3 per cent were professionals).

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "Only up to 3 per cent." Right, well, that's, I'm afraid, been missed out of our translation, Mr. Krgovic. So perhaps you might allow for that before you leap to your feet in indignation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Anyhow, what I was asking you yesterday, which is why I began this, is where you got the figure of 3 per cent from. And you said you thought from the combat readiness report. Can you tell us whether you found it?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I have found it, and I would like the document that you tendered yesterday to be displayed. More specifically, page 71.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just pause. Pause. We'll get up the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's, please, document number P1781.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you say it's page 71 in the B/C/S, do you?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What is it -- what's the number on the top, please. Oh, I see it now. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, it's all right. I think we've got it. That's the right page that you're talking about it, is it?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And it's page 79 in the English. Can you tell us which paragraph? Just read the beginning of the paragraph out.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The actual manning of VRS unit with officers varies greatly, and according to operational formations is as follows." And we must scroll down now because the figures are to be found in the latter part.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Which -- which paragraph? Is that the one beginning, "in total ..."

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just go back for the benefit of the Trial Chamber. When we yesterday discussed the percentage of 3 per cent, you showed the document which stated documents such as 50 per cent, 17 per cent, and so on, but the context is very different. At the beginning of --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... sir, just pause because the right page in English is not there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we go to the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, this is the part I was showing you yesterday, and I dealt with the 1st Krajina Corps. So what do you want to say about that?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to say that the figures you showed and which is different from mine is not what I was speaking about. These figures here show that, for example, the 1st Krajina Corps is -- has a manning level of 50 per cent. But let me answer your question. Where you can find the foundation for my assertion that the greatest number of soldiers were mobilised from the population, that there were very few active-duty professionals. The last -- the last bullet point of this paragraph which start with the words: "In total, in the Army of the RS, of the 14.541 officer establishment posts, 7287, or 51 per cent, are filled with officers, of whom" -- and now the essential bit follows: "1579 are active-duty officers." 1579 out of these 7287. That's a percentage of 22 per cent. Of the 12.032 non-commissioned officers, officers establishment posts, there are 12.942. That is more than planned, which is possible too. But out of these 12.942, only 1190 are active-duty NCOs, or, in terms of percentage, 8 per cent of the overall number. So, if we add that up, 1190 active-duty NCOs and 1579 active-duty officers, we get a number of about 2669. Only they are professionals. Out of the total strength of the army which is something like 80.000 [as interpreted]. That's not even 3 per cent. That's about 1.6 per cent. And that shows that what I state in my report is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I believe that the -- the -- the total number, total strength of the army, is not properly recorded. I believe the witness said 180.000. Maybe you can clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I rather feel that the witness ought to himself have said it. But never mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, believe me, you can -- you can listen to the -- to the audiotape. But ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, Mr. Zecevic, but we have established that the witness should merely be asked to repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. What did you say, General? Did you say, as Mr. Zecevic says, 180.000?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. I said about 180.000 soldiers at the time this analysis was made.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I regret to say, General, I haven't followed with the greatest understanding your mathematical calculations. But just tell me: Where does the figure of 3 per cent appear anywhere? Because you've just said it's not even 3 per cent, it's 1.6. So how did you arrive at 3 per cent?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I stated that the bulk of the army then was -- were mobilised men from the population, and the essence is that there were very few active-duty officers with or without a commission. And I've just found it in this analysis of combat readiness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, found what?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, you said: "I've just found it in this analysis of combat readiness." Do you mean you've found the figure of 3 per cent?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I -- I believe the witness answered and it wasn't recorded. So perhaps the witness should be asked to speak slower so the interprets can interpret what -- his answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: General, you've heard that, which is a sensible, if I may say so, warning, because we've heard this before. It's really important that you don't speak too quickly so the interpreters can keep up. Now, are you referring to the figure of 3 per cent?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stating these figures and this information from the analysis of combat readiness, Ms. Korner, I have proved and confirmed that my assertion that the then-army at the beginning mostly consisted of mobilised men from the reserve force and only a small number of professionals. And I include the percentage of up to 3 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. 22 per cent -- let's go back to the officers. 22 per cent were active officers; correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, 22 per cent active-duty officers calculated against the total number of officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I don't think I'm going to waste more time on this, because the figures speak for themselves. You say that you worked that out as 3 percent, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I want to ask -- General, I want to ask you one question. You said total strength of the army 80.000 -- pardon? 180.000. 180.000. Where do you get that figure from?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think, we find that earlier. There's a total establishment. In fact, I think it's more than that. If Your Honour goes to page 73. Can we have page 73 up on the -- the page. And it's, in B/C/S -- sorry, Your Honours, I'm not quite sure what it is in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may help, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Very grateful, General. You tell me.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Serbian version, it's on page 68.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But then I don't understand - but it's perhaps my lack of understanding, how these figures on page -- what is it, 76 in the English text?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's not the same --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: No. No, the ones we were just --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- analysing a few minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah, it's that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: - how these refer to 180.000. What's the link between?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It doesn't. This is what the General volunteered. It doesn't refer to 180.000 in the previous text. He gave that figure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I mean, if we have to get to a percentage of 180.000, General, how do you -- how do you get that percentage by adding up the numbers that you just added up, page, whatever page it was, the -- the officers and the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Page 80 in the English, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can you explain that to me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I mean, we're -- what we are talking about is the number of non-professional people in the army. And the total of 180.000, how many people were there that were not professional military men; right? So explain that to me, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, answering Ms. Korner's question, I said that in the VRS, for the most part, there were reserve forces that were mobilised. That there wasn't -- that there weren't enough professionals. And on this page, where you see the table, you will see the numbers for the active-duty personnel and the mobilised personnel. The active-duty personnel are officers and non-commissioned officers. If you add up the numbers for the professionals and the mobilised force, you will get 180.000, which is a figure that's mentioned at a number of places in this analysis. And if my math is right --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't get the number of the -- the officers. Could he please repeat.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just stop. General, you're going too fast again. The interpreter missed the number you gave of the officers.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Stop. I'm sorry, General, we're not getting any translation at all now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Apologies. The microphone was off. In the table that we saw at the beginning, it shows that ... Please continue, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I? Ms. Korner, in my previous explanation, I said that in the first document it is clearly stated in the latter part of the document that in the VRS at the time there were 2.669 active-duty officers, or professionals, if you will. And all the rest were reserve forces and the rank and file. These 2.669 represent a percentage of 1.5 of the overall strength of the army mentioned in this analysis which is about 180.000.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, can -- no, but let's have a look at this figure. Can we now look, please, at page 73 in English, and it's 65 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The second table on the B/C/S page, and the only table on the English page, shows what the envisaged establishment strength was and the actual establishment strength. Now, the time that the figures that you have earlier discussed, or talked about, it states, does it not, under total VRS, 214.121.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is there a problem? I'm being waved at for some reason.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Korner, it is quite possible that I was misinterpreted. I said this was page 63. I offered my help with that, or, rather, 68 in the Serbian and not 65. But we may as well go on and comment on page 65, as well, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, that's what I'm asking you to comment. That's, as far as I understand it, the overall total figure of the VRS in -- admittedly, February 1993. We'll go back to the other one you mentioned, if you like. That's at page 76 in English and page -- as I think the page you gave us, 68 in B/C/S. Now, there you see a total of 182.000, which is the actual -- apparently the actual war establishment strength. And it's -- the earlier figure says actual establishment strength. So what's the difference between the two figures, please?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I don't understand the question. What is the difference? I said at the time that as far as I could tell the real establishment was about 180.000. And you can tell that by looking at the other part of this form, where it says manning levels, actual ones, 182.000. And the preceding part of the document tells you about what it should have been by the book, what the establishment was supposed to be in each of the units.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. We fully understand -- I mean, that's what it says. Envisaged and actual. What I'm asking you about - if you can't explain it, then say so, General - is the difference between the figure here, which is shown as the total actual war establishment strength of 182.689, 95.7 per cent of what was intended, and the other figure, if we go back, please, to page 73 in B/C/S and 65 -- sorry, 73 in English and 65 in B/C/S, where it says the actual total was 214.000-odd.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have that in English too, please. Can we pull the image down a little so that we can see the title or the header over Figure 23. Both for the witness's benefit, as well as the Chamber's.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not talking about Figure 23; I'm talking about Figure 24.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Korner, it is true, if you look at a different spot in this table, the figure there is 214.021, that being the actual strength. Why is there a discrepancy between these two figures? We should probably ask whoever processed these figures. Whichever figure you take, and then you take the figure that I spoke about, it only proves my assertion. There were very few professional, commissioned officers in the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But finally, General, because we really have spent a long time on what should have been a very simple point. The bulk of the Yugoslav armies was always made up, was it not, from mobilisations, you told us yesterday?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So there always were only a small percentage of - and I can't give you an exact figure - a small percentage of those who were in a mobilised army who were professional in the sense that they did nothing else but military duties?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the JNA, all those employed there were professional military men. They were employed by the JNA on a permanent basis. There were some soldiers doing their regular military term, if that is what you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. By "professional," I understand the term to mean those whose career is in the military, not those doing national service, and not those who respond to mobilisation orders. Do you agree that is the definition of a professional officer?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And they were always, were they not, in the times of the JNA a small proportion of the actual mobilised army?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact percentage. But if you mean those permanently employed and citizens who came to the JNA to do their regular military term, normally six, seven, eight, or even 12 months, at any rate, the discrepancy was not small. The ratio must have been like this. The units and commands working with those young men had manning levels of up to 100 per cent, all of these professional military officers, covering all the various duties. And there's one thing that I'd like to point out. When the war broke out, company commander level, even battalion commander level, you would have someone occupying a very important post, and sometimes this person was not fully professionally trained as a military man. And these people were now waging war. That is why I said that at the outset there were quite few professional soldiers involved. That was what I was trying to say when I asserted that in my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, well, I really don't want to spend any more time on this, but I was not including those who did their military service. But you've just stated that: "When the war broke out, company commander ... even battalion commander level, you would have someone occupying a very important post," who "was not fully professionally trained?" Can you name, please, anybody that you say when the war broke out was in command of a battalion who was not a professionally trained soldier?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, specific information can be found in the analysis of combat readiness document, when they address issues to do with manning levels of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: My question to you, sir, was whether you could name any officer in command of a battalion who was not a professionally trained soldier --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I object to this line of questioning. Ms. Korner asked the question and the witness pointed her to a source of information. Therefore, if she insists on asking this question, she should perhaps ask him where specifically he found this in the document that he referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, having regard to the witness's declared experience, expertise, or knowledge, I don't see a problem with the question. If he's able to answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But she wants specific names. And the witness said it's something from the analysis document. And again she wants specific names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, I don't see a problem. Unless I'm missing something in your objection. Ms. Korner, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm entitled to ask any question I like. Now, General, for the last time, please, can you name any officer you say was in charge of a battalion when war broke out - and by that I take it you mean June of 1991 - who was not an experienced military officer?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I wasn't talking about June 1991. I'm talking about when the war broke out in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. In April/May 1992, can you name an officer who was in charge of a battalion who was not a professional military officer?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I can't give you a specific name. Nevertheless, there were problems to do with manning levels and particularly establishment posts. I'm sure it's in the document that I referred to, the analysis of combat readiness. It's on the list of documents that I attached to my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, General, I'm sure there is. And may I say, I don't dispute that there were manning problems when the VRS was set up. What I am asking you about is your assertion that so few officers in charge were professional. Now we've dealt with that, and I'd like to move on, please, if at all possible. I want to ask you about something you said yesterday when dealing with this issue, how professional or how many -- what the percentage of professional people were. You said - let me just find it - yes. This is at the bottom of page 23995, when I was putting to you that you were wrong in respect of the 1st Krajina Corps when you said that the person -- most of the personnel was inexperienced and insufficiently trained for war. And you said: "I'm not wrong. I'm an experienced officer with the highest military rank. I know for sure that if they had all been well trained, there would not have been so many problems and so many cases of violation of the international law of war." What were you referring to when you said "so many cases of the violation of the international law of war"?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, it's a well-known fact that in the war in the former Yugoslavia crimes were committed against humanity, or, indeed, violations of international law of war, which was one of the reasons that this Honourable Tribunal was set up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... [microphone not activated] ... yes, but you were talking about, specifically -- It's on. You were talking specifically about the VRS. And so can you tell us what incidents where the VRS were involved in international -- in offences against international humanitarian law? Crimes, sorry. Well, let me put certain incidents to you. Were you referring, for example, to what happened at Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I was referring to the fact that the discipline was poor. Organisation was poor. Manning levels were poor. There was a shortage of professional military officers. So all of these were some of the potential reasons that led to violations of international law of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But what you said was "so many cases of violation." So I'm asking you now what you were thinking about or referring to there. Was it Srebrenica? Was that one of them?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I can't remember whether I said so many or how many. I am certain that I used the word "cases," though. But the one thing that we do know is that quite a number of individuals have already been tried before this Tribunal for violations of international law of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Are you prepared to tell me, General, to what you were referring by that answer yesterday? Which specific incidents, if any?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I wasn't referring to any specific incidents. I was talking in more general terms. Things like that happened. I was against that such cases were tried, and that is precisely what we are discussing today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's move on. Let's go back to your introduction, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have that back up on the screen. 31D2. Page 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's go back to that very same sentence that we've just looked at. It starts: "In conditions of war and armed combat, these documents," namely, the SFRY documents, "were applied to the military and police forces." First of all, how do you know that the SFRY laws applied to police forces?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, all of the forces involved in the war, and I mean the Serbs, the Croats, the Bosniaks, all of them, had the same rules and regulations, both military and police. All of them were unprepared for war. And when the war broke out, the federal rules and regulations were still in force. Nevertheless, all these groups gradually started adopting their own.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, sorry, but the question is simply this. Because you told us earlier you weren't an expert in the police. How do you know what documents applied to the police forces? You haven't studied any documents, had you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can Ms. Korner be specific in this case, because if you look at this particular sentence ... I kindly ask Ms. Korner to pose a question based on this particular page, not mislead the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You state that: "In conditions of war and armed combat, these documents were applied to the military and police forces ..." My question to you is: How do you know they applied to the police force when you did not study the police documents?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, over the last couple of days, we discussed the Law on Internal Affairs, or the Law on Defence, if I remember correctly. There are some transitional provisions there, in some law or other, and it says that federal law provisions shall be applied in those segments not regulated by internal rules, as I said in the paragraph before the one that you quote.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just a moment. First of all, you were never shown the Law on Internal Affairs passed by the Republika Srpska, nor, according to your bibliography, did you look at it before you wrote this report. Now, is that right? No, Mr. Zecevic, I know what he said. I'm entitled to ask these questions without interruption.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I know. I don't want to suggest anything to the witness. But I don't think your question is fair. That is the point. And if the witness can be excused, I can explain why. And it's very clear. You know very well why this is not a fair question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a -- well, Your Honours, I'm afraid to say, it's no good Mr. Zecevic asserting that. I do not know why it's not a fair question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to ask the witness to be escorted outside so I could hear Mr. Zecevic's objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I may. Your Honours, the witness -- Ms. Korner said the following: "In conditions of war" -- this is the question, page 18, 4: "Let's go back to that very same sentence that we've just looked at. It starts: 'In conditions of war and armed combat, these documents,' namely, the SFRY documents, 'were applied to the military and police forces.'" Question: "First of all, how do you know that the SFRY laws applied to police forces?" So on and so forth. And then the witness answers. Now, Your Honours, the SFRY --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, no. No. Your Honours, I'm sorry, could Mr. Zecevic read out the witness's answer, because it's the basis of my following question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: "Ms. Korner, all of the forces involved in the war, and I mean the Serbs, the Croats, the Bosniaks, all of them, had the same rules and regulations, both military and police. All of them were unprepared for war. And when the war broke out, the federal rules and regulations were still in force. Nevertheless, all these groups gradually started adopting their own."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. The question that was put to him, you state, and this is at 18, line 23: "You state that: 'In conditions of war and armed combat, these documents were applied to the military and police forces ...' "My question to you is: How do you know they applied to the police force when you did not study the police documents? "A. Ms. Korner, over the last couple of days, we discussed the Law on Internal Affairs, or the Law on Defence, if I remember correctly. There are some transitional provisions there, in some law or other, and it says ... federal law provisions shall be applied ..." Now, I was going to go through each of those sections because he refers, first of all, to the Law on Internal Affairs, and I am entitled to ask the question that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, my -- then my -- I -- I wasn't given the opportunity to state my objection. My objection, Your Honours, was the following: The expert speaks in his expert opinion. He speaks about the federal laws, the laws of the former Yugoslavia, so the federal laws. Now, the question by Ms. Korner is directed to the laws of RS. So therefore - because this is not a legal expert, this is the army expert - she should point out the distinction or at least clarify with the witness what is the -- what is the question. Whether the question pertains to the federal law or the laws of the Republika Srpska. That is what I think is unfair. That was my objection. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But I -- unless I'm wholly missing your point, Mr. Zecevic, I -- I don't see how the approach -- your approach may have been different, but the approach that Ms. Korner is taking is objectionable [sic], and she should be permitted to continue. I -- I don't see a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours. Thank you very much. And I'm sorry I made this intervention.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: No apology is necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, it is, Your Honour. I was accused of deliberately doing something that I knew to be unfair, and I think an apology is due. Can I say one other thing, Your Honour. This witness is proceeding incredibly slowly; largely from what, I would suggest, are wholly unwarranted interruptions from the Defence. And if it goes on like this, this witness will be taking until Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Why I indicated that I didn't think it was necessary for Mr. Zecevic to apologise is that he perceived that the approach that you were taking is one where the witness would not have been as helpful as he could have been. I didn't take your ancillary point about your -- his suggestion that you were deliberately misleading the witness. So could we have the witness back on the stand. And I suppose I should add to the observation that Ms. Korner has just made, that whereas while the Chamber, of course, is -- appreciates the zeal of Defence counsel in the interests of their clients, counsel -- Defence counsel should be assured that the Chamber is alive to the necessity to protect the witness from any unfairness on the part of the -- of the counsel who is now on her feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right, General, this is a simple question: Have you ever looked at the Law on Internal Affairs passed in March of 1982 which regulates the conduct of police during the course of its duties?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, to explain, and that was my task, the use of the police in combat activities, I perused military rules and regulations because that was the only way I could shed light on the problem. I did not deal with the Law on Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Well, come on to it later, but as you yourself pointed out in your paragraph 22, I think it is, it was quite complicated to work out the role of the police in combat because the only law that seems to deal specifically with it, at that period of time, is the Law on National Defence, passed in 1982; is that right? No, you needn't look up the paragraph, General, because we're going to come to it. But as a general, overall picture, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct. I wasn't listening carefully, but I believe you're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, it's important, General, not to start flicking through your report. I promise you that I'm not going to miss out anything that you consider important. And in any event, Mr. Krgovic has a chance to re-examine you. So please listen to the question, and don't go through your report. Now, can we just look at two other matters, please, in this introductory paragraph. You say that - going back to the same sentence: "In conditions of war and armed combat, these documents were applied to military and police forces which consisted of mobilised people, only up to 3 per cent were professionals, who had a very low level of discipline." Who had a very low level of discipline? The professionals, the reservists, the mobilised forces, who?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I meant, and gave a general assessment of the situation, that the level of discipline in the VRS was low.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And can you tell us, please, what you base that assessment on; is it in a document? You're talking to other people? Or your own personal experience in the months until you left?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I believe that such an assessment can also be found in the analysis of the combat readiness of the VRS. The information I found there, that, during one year only, about 4.000 criminal reports were filed, speaks for itself as regards the level of discipline in that army at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Then you said: "We go back to the untrained and inexperienced commanding officers." And I dealt with that yesterday. "... poor internal communications." What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, it is a well-known fact that in every war communication is difficult for a number of reasons, but there was also poor communication between individual commanders --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yeah, I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- at various levels.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, every war may be every war. Specifically this is meant to be dealing with the VRS. Why do you say there was poor internal communication?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I say that communication lines were interrupted, and that's a well-known fact, I believe. Roads were blocked. It wasn't possible to go to the units and exercise control, see what the situation was like, and so on. I believe I know what war is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, yes. But you may know what war is, but this is specific. On what do you base your assertion that communication -- that there was poor internal communication, in other words, presumably from the lower units to the brigades, to the corps, to the Main Staff? Are you just guessing because of what you say is your knowledge of war?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not guessing. I'm making an assertion. And I stand by what I stated here, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I know you're making an assertion, but I'm asking you on what you base this assertion. And we're going to look at some documents in a moment. But I'm just asking you now: On what do you base this assertion?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said, on my experience and on the documents I read. I cannot remember specifically which document that was. But there must be instances of poor internal communications between individual commanders who, for example, were appointed by Crisis Staffs but weren't even JNA members, although there were JNA members who weren't well-accepted in the field. And examples of that can be found in documents. I'm sure that some of these documents are mentioned in my bibliography.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you don't, actually. But the -- can you see the importance, I hope, General, for further reference, of footnoting, as you write a report, what you're basing it on. All right. Let's have a look at some of the documents that relate to the 1st Krajina Corps, for example.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we have up on the screen, please, document number -- it's 20 -- 65 ter 20225. And it's tab 12.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It is, in fact, the -- as we can see, the duty team daily notes on the situation on the battle-field and in the zone of responsibility, and it comes from the 1st Krajina Corps. Were you aware --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Is Ms. Korner testifying? Where is that, that this document is 1st Krajina Corps? In the document, can we find the reference?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is there a dispute that this document comes from the 1st Krajina Corps? And it becomes absolutely apparently as you go through it. If there's a dispute, I'll certainly call a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know that this document was disclosed for cross-examination, so the Prosecutor should ask the witness if he has seen it and if he can conclude what it's about. I cannot tell, based on what I see, that this is a document of the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document, along with the whole of the 1st Krajina Corps collection, has been in EDS for some time. It has not been used so far because it was not thought necessary to use it so far. In case the Defence had not been through it, we disclosed it in advance of cross-examination. And if, as I say, there is a dispute that this is a 1st Krajina Corps document, then I will call a witness to deal with the recovery of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but, madam, you are testifying when you're saying this is a document of the 1st Krajina Corps. That is not appropriate. You should show something to the witness which -- out of which it clearly follows that it's a document of the 1st Krajina Corps, instead of making an assertion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's the whole point. If Mr. Krgovic is genuinely disputing that this is a document of the 1st Krajina Corps, then, as I said, I will call evidence. I will move on. I will not ask about this document until I've called evidence to show that, although by reading through the document you can tell it's the 1st Krajina Corps. But that's what I will do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Krgovic, your objection -- your observation - let me use that word - that it had not been disclosed to the Defence previously, what do you say about Ms. Korner's response? Because the -- the -- whereas as I understand the -- your objection to be that she is now saying what this document is although it is a matter in dispute, what her response is that she would -- and these are my words, not hers, is that the document speaks for itself and that save for your objection now voiced, there would have been no dispute as to what this document is. So I come back to my basic question about -- she says you've had it and ought to have seen and ought to be familiar with its contents. That's essentially what she's saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. But when Ms. Korner says that this is a document of the 1st Krajina Corps, we see some dates at the beginning, and those dates were from a time when there was no 1st Krajina Corps. And that is the point. The document -- the fact that the document was disclosed in EDS does not mean that we are necessarily familiar with the document. That's why I cannot say or readily accept that this a document of the 1st Krajina Corps, given that according to me it does not follow from the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... so now we understand and Ms. Korner appreciates that there is a dispute about this, and as she said, it's something to which she will have to return.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, she may ask questions and establish through the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... no, no, first of all, Your Honour, we sent this. It's not right that it's just on EDS, because having read his report it was clear that I was going to be asking about communications. We disclosed, even though it was on EDS, in advance of even handing over our list of documents. And Mr. Smith is just looking up the batch in which we disclosed it. Second, and I couldn't believe I was hearing what I heard, the dispute is that it's the 1st Krajina Corps which wasn't in existence when it began. That's absolutely correct. It was the 5th Krajina Corps of the JNA, transformed into the 1st Krajina Corps after the declaration of the VRS. And the documents, as Mr. Krgovic knows, all the documents, were recovered when the headquarters of the 1st Krajina Corps were searched in 1998 in Banja Luka. But, Your Honours, as I say, I'm perfectly happy. I will move on to another document. I will ask for Your Honours' leave to call evidence after lunch -- after lunch. After the break -- to establish that's where it comes from, and then we can go back to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It was actually, in fact, it was a footnote in Mr. Brown's report and it was disclosed to the Defence in 2008. Is there anything else I need to say on this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, where did you see the dates on this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] -- we'll go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you look at the first page, you can see that the date is the 20th of April. And then when you move on, it's the 22nd of February, 1992. 0941336 is the page reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well then. But do you still wish to contest that this is what it appears to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't have a problem with that. But the Prosecutor must somehow establish through the witness that it's a document of the 5th Krajina Corps. Whether it was recovered in the archives of the 1st Krajina Corps or of the archives of the VRS is not so important. But when Ms. Korner makes a reference, the reference should be appropriate, and the Prosecutor mustn't be allowed to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Obviously, Mr. Krgovic, the witness will most likely be unable to confirm that this is what it appears to be, because he says that he hasn't seen it. So the issue now before us is whether you insist that Ms. Korner should call another witness to confirm --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In that case, with Your Honours' leave, maybe tomorrow morning I'll do it, and I'll come back to this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's look at some other documents, please, that deal with the communication that you say, the -- the poor internal communication. Can we look now, please, at document -- I'm now going to show you a series of reports from the 1st Krajina Corps which I don't think there can be any dispute about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: P1809, please. And it's 23 of the Prosecution list. Sorry, 23 -- it's 23A.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this document, first of all, have you ever seen this one before?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have. A great many documents are cited in Mr. Brown's footnotes. But I have no problem with commenting on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no, just a moment, please. Forget that you read Mr. Brown's report over the weekend and that it was clear that he had looked at all these documents. I'm asking whether you had looked at this particular document before, whether you'd been given it or were aware of it.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, it's not referenced in your report, is it?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To answer that, I would have to look at my report. I don't really remember all the documents that I used. It was six months ago, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, you can check your report on the break, if you like. All right. Now, this is a document, do you agree, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, Ms. Korner, since you're about to go into this, should we take the break?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, while the witness is ushered in, if I may just make a couple of comments concerning the transcript, some clarifications in the transcript. On page 21, I made an inappropriate comment, and I would like to put on the record that I apologise to Ms. Korner. I completely misunderstood her question and I don't think it was appropriate, and, moreover, I was totally wrong. That's why I wanted to put this on the record. The second thing is that I was recorded as saying "I'm sorry I made this intervention." What I meant to say was that I'm sorry that I caused this pause in the cross-examination and need of the witness to leave the courtroom, which took some time. That is what I wanted to say. Thank you very much, Your Honours. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I thank Mr. Zecevic for his very handsome apology, if I may say so. And, of course, we will understand in the heat of the moment sometimes things get heated. Can I just go back, however, to the document which we say comes from the 1st Krajina Corps. Mr. Zecevic has had an opportunity to look at it over the adjournment, as indeed I have, and -- in more detail, and I would suggest it's as plain as a pikestaff it's a corps document, and I wonder whether Mr. Zecevic might now withdraw his objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic or Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. Mr. Krgovic, not Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, looking at this, I've had a look, there are references there to some units that were part of the 5th Corps or the 1st Krajina Corps, as the case may be. I don't wish to make this any more difficult than necessary in a procedural sense, but the essence of my objection is: When Ms. Korner asks the witness a question, when she makes reference to a particular document, can she please tell him such and such a document without necessarily suggesting what it is. That is the essence of my objection. Everything else stems from that objection. As far as this is concerned, I'm happy to withdraw my objection. But we would like to have a very specific reference in as far as possible when a document is quoted. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, thank you. In fact, I think it's a document that I'm going to have to invite the General to have a look at again overnight, because it's a lengthy document. So I'll come back to it probably tomorrow morning. Yes, thank you, Your Honours, that's all that I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Tomorrow afternoon, I know. This week is really confusing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Could the witness be conducted back to the stand, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, General, before the break we were about to look at this document. Now, you can't remember whether you've ever seen this document before. I would suggest you probably haven't. But it's the sort of report that you're very familiar with, isn't it? It's the report by an assistant commander for morale, guidance, and legal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we look at the last page, please, in both English and B/C/S. Sorry, not the last page. It's the penultimate -- second page in B/C/S and fourth page in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's a report signed by Colonel Milutin Vukelic, assistant commander for morale, guidance, and legal affairs. First, did you know him?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, a person by that name was a lecturer at the high political school in the JNA when I started attending before the war. This is something that I've already told you about. So if we're talking about the same person, in that case, yes, I do know him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I have no idea whether he taught. But is he now dead, this person you're talking about? because I would suggest to you this Colonel Vukelic is.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of that. And if that indeed is the case, I can only say I'm very sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go back, please, then, to the contents of this report briefly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So back to the first page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this is Colonel Vukelic giving an overview of the political and security situation in the Bosnian Krajina. And he deals in the first paragraph, as we can see, with the beginnings of the -- the -- well, he talks about the present situation, started after the energetic involvement of the Serbian Republic army in the area of Kljuc, Sanski Most. He goes on to deal with Hambarine. Does the attack on Hambarine mean anything to you, General? Do you know anything about it? Or Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about it, but I wasn't there and I wasn't involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. I know you weren't there and I know you weren't involved. I'm asking you whether you know the details of this operation at all from your preparations for this report.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I didn't analyse events or, indeed, documents that were produced on the ground. My primary task was to analyse the rules and regulations in order to prove how it was possible to use police in combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. As we've already established, and we'll go on with it, your report goes a great deal further than that and in particularly in the introduction.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page, please, in English. And I believe it's -- we're still on the same page - yes - in ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He then talks about Prijedor being under the control of the Serbian Ministry of Interior and "our own armed formations." He talks about Vlasic, the political situation in Bosanska Gradiska, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we go to the next page in B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No major changes in Derventa. And a light brigade is being formed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Next page, please, in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And there we see he's talking about conscripts. "The Autonomous Region of Krajina Assembly has taken all possible measures to remove from important posts those persons who have failed to meet their obligations," so on and so forth. "Most of the officials relieved of office are Muslims and Croats, but there are also some Serbian degenerates." I know you didn't write this report. Can you tell us what you understand him to be saying when he's referring to "Serbian degenerates"? General?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I don't quite see that in the original, not the word "degenerate." If we're talking about the paragraph that begins with the following words: "The AR Bosnian Krajina assembly has taken all possible measures," and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's just make sure the translation's correct. Could you read out the last sentence of that paragraph so we can get a translation.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, the last sentence of the paragraph reads: "Most of those relieved of their duties are Muslims and Croats, but the group also includes Serb misfits or renegades."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: It's a term that's quite ambivalent and very difficult to interpret.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Well -- sorry, I think what the interpreter's said has just actually not -- been missed out of the transcript as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] "Misfits or renegades."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "Mis--" right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, what do you -- well, as I say, I agree you didn't write this report, but can you, from your experience at this period, this is May, tell us what he was referring to by "Serb misfits or renegades"?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, when we use this word "izrod," normally we refer to a person who is not a patriot, not loyal to his own people. This means that the persons that's described did not comply with certain rules or regulations or, indeed, refused to join certain defensive operations or refused to be involved in the defence of the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Next paragraph, and it's worth perhaps reading this one in full. "Primarily due to exceptional combat readiness, but also the patience of the troops, the positions previously secured and relative peace have been preserved in the Western Slavonian theatre of war. After the arrival of the UNPROFOR forces, we expect to have all our forces from that area engaged in the Bosnian Krajina theatre of war in the coming days, thus strengthening and securing the endangered territory of the Serbian Republic of BH." Do you accept that, here, Colonel Vukelic is explaining that there are going to be battled-seasoned troops coming to reinforce the troops already in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I am really unable to answer that question. I'm afraid it's an interpretation issue yet again. As far as I can tell, by looking at the original, the original reads: "Over the next few days, we expect that all of our forces from this area will be sent to the Bosanska Krajina theatre of war, following the arrival of UNPROFOR, thereby reinforcing and securing the area of the Serbian Republic of BH which is currently at risk." I don't see the involvement of the two armies or anything like that. I'm not sure I understood your question correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: General, it may well be an interpretation problem. I asked you whether from that paragraph it was clear that the troops who were at this time in the Krajina were going to be reinforced by troops coming from Western Slavonia who had - I said battled-seasoned - but who had been in battle?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, that's not what I see here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, I suppose you better tell us what you do see. What is your interpretation of this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have read it out loud already, and all I can tell is they appear to be expecting that those forces would be engaged in the Bosanska Krajina theatre of war over the following days. There is no reference to any other forces there from Western Slavonia that I can see.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on, then, please. Could you look at the next page, and let's see if you accept that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Next page in English, and it's the same page in B/C/S. Maybe this will make it clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "Krajina troops tested in the Western Slavonian theatre of war will form the core of safety and security in the Bosnia [sic] Krajina ..." Does the word "tested in the Western Slavonian theatre of war" to you suggest that they have been fighting?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, if my impression is correct, and I did look at the last page of this document, this report was meant for the subordinate units. We have the assistant commander for morale --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, I'm going to come on to exactly who this went to, but please just concentrate on that paragraph. Now, does that suggest to you that the troops who were arriving had been in battle?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And you see, it doesn't square, does it, with your assertions that these troops were untrained, inadequate, if you like, non-professional soldiers?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, this assertion is only in reference to a part of the Krajina Corps, a part of its composition. If you look at the VRS as a whole, at the time, and we're looking at late May, there were a total of seven other operative components. It's impossible to take only one of these and, based on that limited sample, claim that all the other components had the same sort of battle seasoning or company experience in combat that you claim they did have.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I'm not suggesting that for one moment, General. I accept entirely that not all the corps that were formed had the same level of manpower, equipment, and professional soldiers as did the 1st Krajina Corps. But the 1st Krajina Corps, I'm going to suggest to you, is what you should have been looking at, given the terms your report. Now, can we turn, please, to the distribution list. Is it right that the distribution list is for those units or officials for whom this report is intended? Is that right, General?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, as a rule, each document should have a list of addressees.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah. And it's the persons who are to be affected by the contents of the document or who are to be informed; is that right? I say "persons." Units, I should say.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. If, indeed, the document reaches all of the units named in the list, and if the commanders of these units are able to have the documents delivered to all of the soldiers out there, some in the trenches and some out in the woods, if all of that applies, in that case, what you say is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's another point, isn't it? This is very early on in the conflict, and there's a full report about everything, in summary, that's been happening over this period from Colonel Vukelic distributed to all the subordinate units; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's leave that document and let's, please, go to a series of reports around the same time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Please can we look next at document P1745.7, tab 24.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a -- sorry -- a 1st Krajina Corps report, is that right, which is reporting or it is a report, I'm sorry, to the 1st Krajina Corps, I think, on what's called the elimination of the Green Berets in the wider area of Kozarac village? And it discusses that. And then in paragraph 2 it says: "Participating in the armed conflict on our side were components of the 343rd Motorised Brigade (an enlarged motorised battalion) supported by two 105-millimetre Howitzer batteries and one M84 tank squadron." Was the M84 a modern tank?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, at the beginning, possibly due to the interpretation, I believe you said this was a report sent to the corps. What I see when I look at this document is that it is a report which the corps command is sending to the Main Staff of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You're quite right. It's my mistake. It's from the 1st Krajina Corps to the Main Staff. Now can we go back to the question I asked. Is the M84 a modern tank?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: M84 is a modern tank. Nevertheless, may I just add that it is by no means forbidden to get these involved in combat. The only thing that is banned is everything that runs counter to international law of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not -- I think it's right that you are unaware, General, of the detail - I think you've said this already - you were unaware of the detail of what happened in Kozarac at the end of May; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can you tell us, please, how many are in a tank squadron?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There should be two in a tank squadron, as far as I know. But obviously it all depends on the manning levels of the units in question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, is it two or more -- or may it be more than two? I mean, General, you're the expert on weaponry and military things in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could Ms. Korner please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How many --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Or allow the witness to read the specific part, because I think that it's -- the word "squad" is slightly differently translated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: End of paragraph 2, what does it say?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, this reads: "A platoon of M84 tanks." A platoon is a unit that's one level higher than a squad, if I understood the interpreters correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can you tell us, please, how many people are in a platoon of tanks?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number of people in any unit is established in the book of military establishment so that the number varies. But there can be 20 to 40 people in a squad.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: A squad or a platoon?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: A platoon. Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And how many tanks?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A platoon can have four to six tanks, in theory.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Going on, then, to this report -- through this report. It talks about, in paragraph 4, overall results. Eighty to a hundred Green Berets killed and about 1.500 captured. In your experience, in your military experience, General, is that a large number to be captured, of fighting men, Green Berets?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Korner, that's relative. I don't know how combat operations went. But in item 2 of this report, I see that some components of the 343rd Motorised Brigade took part, which is rather vague. We don't know which components. They were reinforced by a battalion and supported by two Howitzer batteries and a tank platoon. So speaking about the number of people captured in combat, it's a relative number.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, would you -- relative to what? Would you agree that it's -- it's -- it must have been an imbalance in the size of the forces to allow 1.500, allegedly, fighting men to have been captured?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, that need not always be the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we then just quickly go over the page in this report, please, because we see there the 1st Krajina Corps is listing its strength, going back to what we said this morning. This is in May. And I suppose I should have asked you this before, General: Had you seen this document before you wrote your report?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, if we look very briefly, please, at this, we see that according to this report they have 92 per cent, I think it is -- no, sorry. They have 86 per cent of the officers they should have. The command unit is overstaffed, apparently, 138. The scout, 99 per cent. Radio reconnaissance platoon is quite low. But, as I say, going through this quickly. Overstaffed is the nuclear biological chemical defence company; 7, overstaffed is the communications; 8, well overstaffed is the military police. And then so on and so forth. Do you see those figures for May?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see them, Ms. Korner, and I'll gladly comment when you let me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly. You can say what you like.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, it is possible that something is being misinterpreted. I don't think that this is your intention. Possibly you don't understand me. This is not [Realtime translation read in error "this is"] the manning level I am discussing in my report. What you see here is the manning level according to the military establishment book. Here, you cannot see who the active-duty officers are and who the reserve forces are. In the analysis of combat readiness of the VRS, which includes the entire army, I found the information that there were only 2669 [Realtime translation read in error "26069"] active-duty officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, line -- page 43, 14, I believe the witness's answer was in negative, was in negative. "Not." Not affirmative. I don't want to ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, he said "this is not." Maybe you can clarify.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I'm sorry, he said, in line 14: "Possibly you don't understand me. This is ... the manning level I have been discussing in my report."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. Sorry, line 14: "Possibly you don't understand me -- " Oh I see, "this is not." I follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: General, did you say "this is not the manning level I discussed in my report"?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly, Ms. Korner. This overview presents a different type of manning with regard to the military establishment book. From this, you cannot tell how many active-duty officers there are and how many reserve forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I agree, they don't specify. But they're saying these -- this is the force which is available to us, aren't they, effective strength?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And if we just -- could we go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, but there is a mistake with the number. On page 45 -- 43, it's line 20, it was recorded "26069." I think you can clarify that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right, General. You told us a little bit -- way back that there were "In the analysis of combat readiness ... I found the information that there were only 26069 active-duty officers." What was the figure that you say you found?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I said 2669. And let me add, in order to clarify. This is only about the manning level, whereas I was talking about the quality of that manning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, as I think I put to you yesterday, the 343rd Motorised Brigade --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can we go to the next page in English, please, number 12.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- was led by a Colonel Arsic, who, I suggest to you, was a highly experienced professional officer, and, as we can see, had available to it - accepting that some reservists may not have been called up - some 4.574 ordinary squadees, soldiers. Actually, sorry, 5.415, because it was overmanned. Do you agree that's what they had available to them in that one brigade?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree, Ms. Korner. But these 5.000 soldiers must be viewed in relation to the 600 officers up there, out of whom not all are active-duty officers, because that's the relation I keep talking about. I'm not opposing you when you say that they had many men.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we leave that document, please, and move, purely on the subject of communication, to document, please, P411.29, at tab 31. And let's try and do this fairly quickly. Three days after his last report, on the 27th of May, Colonel Vukelic writes another report. Now, we don't have a distribution list for this one. But, again, within three days, he's reporting about what's going on in the AOR of the 1st Krajina Corps. And in the third paragraph, or second paragraph, we see enemy forces. Third paragraph deals with what's happening in the Banja Luka region and a proportion -- sorry. "A portion of the Muslim and Croatian population is moving out, and the region of Bosnian Krajina has issued a decision to facilitate such departures, providing that the Serbs from Central Bosnia and places with predominantly Muslim and Croatian populations were also allowed to move out. Those departing will not be allowed to return?" Would you accept, General, that is Colonel Vukelic reporting on the political machinations, if that's the right word, that were going on in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, it is very difficult for me to comment on this document because this is a report. This is not an order. We cannot tell from this who it is that allows or disallows anything, whether this is the position of these people there or that of the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. I -- I'm not suggesting -- I'm so sorry; you misunderstood. I'm not, for the moment, suggesting that's what the corps command is saying. I'm suggesting that this is Colonel Vukelic reporting on what's happening with the Banja Luka political authorities. Do you agree that's right?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Korner, it's hard for me to agree, because this paragraph starts with the words "in the Banja Luka region ..." and then some events are mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's -- I'll deal with that. You mentioned in part of your report what you described as municipal authorities having an influence. However, it's correct, isn't it, that you've not looked at a single document emanating from the Crisis Staffs, in particular, the ARK -- the Autonomous Region of Krajina Regional Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm under oath, Ms. Korner, and it's very difficult for me to remember the documents that I used when drafting my report. But they are listed in the bibliography at the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, take it from me, there's no reference to a single Crisis Staff document, certainly not from the ARK Crisis Staff, and I don't believe - I'll double-check that - from any other. Were you shown by either Mr. Krgovic or Mr. Cvijetic any Crisis Staff documents when you got here?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly, madam. I cannot be specific, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, we'll come to some later. All right. And then just, as I say, going very quickly through it. Colonel Vukelic reports on the various areas that come within the AOR of the 1st Krajina Corps? You hadn't seen this document before, had you?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Let's move, please, to the next document -- documents for all around this period.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we look now, please, at 65 ter 619, at tab 32A.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is the 6th of June. And this is the 1st Krajina Corps reporting again directly to the Main Staff. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree, Ms. Korner.
